notes: \cpara{Credits Gillian Russell's essay, later published in \textsc{Martial Arts and Philosophy: Beating and Nothingness} (Open Court, 2010). I checked the quotations below against the penultimate draft on Russell's website, which runs to twelve numbered pages.}

\cpara{Quotes Russell's opening: a teacher told the class that three years of punching the air would let them kill a bull with one blow, and the eleven-year-old Russell believed it. ``Viciousness'' is used in the old sense, ``possessing of vices''.}
\cpara{Says the essay's observations generalize ``amazingly'', and summarizes them in seven points. The summary follows the essay's sections in order, and its quotations match the draft closely.}

\cpara{Corrects the author's own memory of the essay, openly. The essay does make a nearby point. In judo, Russell writes, ``either you manage to throw your opponent, or you don't'', so it leaves ``relatively little room for pretence''; odd beliefs do better in arts ``such as aikido, where there is usually less competitive randori''.}

\cpara{A history of the martial arts from memory, with no source: when real fights decided things, people knew who the masters were. ``A Sense That More Is Possible'', posted the same day, relies on the same history; see the note there.}
\cpara{The decline, with YouTube videos as the evidence. Videos of black belts losing today show that some lose; with no comparison to the past, they do not show that things ``went downhill''.}

\cpara{The ki master, from memory. A commenter linked a video two days later, ``Kiai Master vs MMA''. That is probably the case of Yanagi Ryuken (``Kiai Master Ryukerin'' in some accounts, says Wikipedia's ``Touchless knockout''). In Skeptoid's account (episode 189, 2010), he ``offered \$5000 to any modern Mixed Martial Arts athlete who could beat him'', and was beaten in front of Japanese television cameras.}

\cpara{The conclusion: every risk factor carries over to a ``rationality dojo''. The post asserts this without going through the factors. Data poverty is the one the author argues for at length elsewhere (``A Sense That More Is Possible'' calls verifying training ``the essential, blocking obstacle'').}

\cfact{The essay the post summarizes offers partial answers that the summary leaves out. Where a technique cannot be tested whole, ``we can test and practice aspects of our techniques without testing all aspects of the technique at once''. And deference to a teacher becomes a vice, Russell argues, when the line between ``justified epistemic deference'' and ``unjustified epistemic deference'' blurs.}
